Favour
fā'vur
n. (kind regard, goodwill; rendering Hebrew chen and ratson, Greek charis)
From the Latin favor, from faveo, to be kind toward. The Authorized Version keeps the older British spelling. Hebrew chen is grace or acceptance in another's eyes, and ratson is good pleasure or acceptance — the term used of a sacrifice God receives.

Biblical Definition

Favour is regard freely given, and in Scripture it moves in two directions. Godward, it is the Old Testament's ordinary word for grace: Noah found chen in the eyes of the LORD, and the noun rendered favour here is the same the New Testament renders grace. The Psalmist measures it against wrath and finds it decisive: “For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life” (Psalm 30:5). Manward, favour is the good regard of one's neighbours, and Scripture treats it as a real good, worth seeking honestly: “So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man” (Proverbs 3:4). Luke says the same of our Lord's boyhood — he “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man” (Luke 2:52) — which shows that seeking to be well regarded is not in itself the sin of men-pleasing. But the word carries a warning in its other main use, where favour means charm or attractiveness: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). The charm that wins regard is the very thing that may mislead, and the fear of the LORD is set against it as the durable ground of praise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Kind regard freely given. Hebrew chen is the Old Testament word for grace; favour with men is a real good honestly sought, though the charm that wins it is called deceitful.

expand to see more

FAVOR, FAVOUR, n. [L. favor, from faveo, to be kind to.] Kind regard; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition.

2. Support; defense; vindication; as, to speak in favor of a friend.

3. A kind act or office; kindness done or granted; benevolence shown.

4. Object of kind regard; the person favored; also, grace or beauty of countenance.

5. In Scripture, the free grace of God; as, in his favor is life, Psa. 30; Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord, Gen. 6.

Key Scripture

Psalm 30:5 — "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."

Proverbs 3:4 — "So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man."

Luke 2:52 — "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man."

Proverbs 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Modern Corruption

Favour now suggests partiality — the unfair leg-up, the connection that jumped the queue. Scripture's favour is unmerited by definition, which is not injustice but grace, since none had a claim in the first place.

expand to see more

The modern suspicion of favour comes from a real concern about corruption in human dealings, where showing favour usually means denying someone else their due. But the objection cannot be transferred to God without destroying the gospel, because no creature is owed anything, and where nothing is owed nothing is withheld. Divine favour is not God preferring some over others who had a claim; it is God giving to some what none could claim. Romans anticipates the complaint and answers it: is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid.

There is also a prosperity distortion running the other way, in which favour means smooth circumstances — the parking space, the promotion — so that trouble becomes evidence of lost favour. Psalm 30:5 says favour is life while anger is a moment, not that the favoured man never weeps; weeping may endure for a night. The principle to recover is that the favour Scripture chiefly means is the settled acceptance of a sinner in Christ, which does not fluctuate with the week's news.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chen is grace or acceptance in another's eyes, from chanan, to stoop in kindness; ratson is good pleasure, the acceptance of a sacrifice. Greek charis covers both and becomes the New Testament word for grace.

expand to see more

Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour, acceptance; what Noah found in the eyes of the LORD.

Hebrew ratson (H7522) — goodwill, acceptance, delight; used of an offering God receives.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness; favour bound by promise rather than by whim.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace, favour; the Septuagint's regular rendering of chen.

Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure, goodwill; the angels' word over Bethlehem.

Usage

"Of divine favour set against momentary anger: his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life (Psalm 30:5)."

"Of the good regard of God and neighbour: Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52)."

"Of charm as an unreliable ground of praise: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain (Proverbs 31:30)."
